---
title: "The model"
---

## One representation throughout

Every component of the package speaks a single representation: `TFModel`, a
continuous-time transfer function stored as polynomial coefficients
(descending powers of `s = j2πf`) with leading denominator coefficient
normalised to 1.  This mirrors the `{num, den}` convention of the original
`sysIDlib` engine — validated math from prior LIGO work is reused without
coordinate-change errors.

The representation is:

$$
G(s;\theta) = \frac{b_0 s^m + b_1 s^{m-1} + \cdots + b_m}
                   {s^n + a_1 s^{n-1} + \cdots + a_n}
$$

where the parameter vector θ = (b₀, …, b_m, a₁, …, a_n) is what the Fisher
information and the estimator operate on.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why normalise the leading denominator?

Normalising the leading denominator coefficient to 1 removes one degree
of freedom (the overall gain is absorbed into the numerator), so the
Jacobian ∂G/∂θ has no null directions and the Fisher matrix is full-rank
for any well-excited measurement.
:::

## Construction

Construct a `TFModel` however is natural for your system:

```python
from system_ident.model import TFModel
import numpy as np

# ── from (f0 [Hz], Q) resonances ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Suspension mode at 1 Hz, Q = 20; optionally with additional resonances.
g1 = TFModel.from_resonances([(1.0, 20.0)], gain=1.0)

# Double pendulum: 0.6 Hz Q20 + 1.5 Hz Q30
g2 = TFModel.from_resonances([(0.6, 20.0), (1.5, 30.0)], gain=250.0)

# ── from zeros / poles / gain ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# Fabry–Pérot cavity pole at 100 Hz
wc = 2 * np.pi * 100.0
g3 = TFModel.from_zpk(zeros=[], poles=[-wc], gain=wc)

# ── from a raw {num, den} dict ────────────────────────────────────────────
# Matches the format stored by the sysIDlib MATLAB code
g4 = TFModel.from_dict({"num": [1.0], "den": [1.0, 6.28, 39.5]})
```

All constructors normalise to the leading-den-1 convention before storing.

## Evaluation and differentiation

```python
freq = np.linspace(0.1, 5.0, 400)

G_complex = g2.eval(freq)          # complex array, shape (400,)
G_abs     = np.abs(G_complex)      # magnitude
G_phase   = np.angle(G_complex)    # phase [rad]

# Jacobian: (n_params × n_freq) complex array
# Used by fisher_matrix() and parameter_covariance()
J = g2.jacobian(freq)
```

`g.jacobian(freq)` returns ∂G/∂θ — the per-parameter sensitivity of the response
at every frequency. It is evaluated by **central finite differences** on the
stacked `[num, den]` parameter vector (validated bit-for-bit against the legacy
`sysIDlib` engine), and it is the critical quantity feeding both the Fisher
calculation and the Gauss-Newton step of the maximum-likelihood fit. Where a
parameter spans orders of magnitude, a per-parameter `logflag` switches the column
to the derivative with respect to a *fractional* change, which keeps the
information matrix well conditioned near sharp resonances.

::: {.callout-note}
## Fitting in physical parameters: `ResonatorModel`

`TFModel` is the canonical representation, but mechanical resonances are far
better conditioned when estimated as **physical** `(f0, Q, gain)` parameters
rather than expanded polynomial coefficients.  `ResonatorModel` provides exactly
that: a product of second-order resonances whose gradient `∂H/∂f0` *directly*
moves a peak in frequency, so a Gauss-Newton / MAP step can relocate a resonance
that sits away from the prior — which coefficient-space fitting cannot.  It
exposes the same four-method protocol (`params`, `jacobian`, `eval`,
`with_params`) and a `to_tf()` bridge back to `TFModel` for discretisation and
Foton export, so the Fisher, estimator, and designer machinery is unchanged.
:::

## Plotting a model

```{python}
#| label: fig-bode-model
#| fig-cap: "Bode-style magnitude plot of a 2-mode suspension model (0.6 Hz Q20, 1.5 Hz Q30)."
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from system_ident.model import TFModel

model = TFModel.from_resonances([(0.6, 20.0), (1.5, 30.0)], gain=250.0)
freq  = np.linspace(0.05, 5.0, 800)
resp  = np.abs(model.eval(freq))

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=freq, y=resp,
    mode='lines',
    line=dict(color='#1F8AC0', width=2.5),
    hovertemplate='%{x:.3f} Hz   |G| = %{y:.4f}<extra></extra>',
))

for f0, label in [(0.6, 'f₁ = 0.6 Hz'), (1.5, 'f₂ = 1.5 Hz')]:
    idx = np.argmin(np.abs(freq - f0))
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=freq[idx], y=resp[idx],
        text=f'<b>{label}</b>',
        showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, arrowsize=1.1,
        arrowcolor='rgba(200,151,58,0.75)',
        ax=50, ay=-40,
        font=dict(size=11, color='#C8973A', family='Outfit, sans-serif'),
    )

fig.update_layout(
    template='plotly_white',
    height=340, margin=dict(l=60, r=20, t=20, b=55),
    font=dict(family='Outfit, Inter, sans-serif', size=12),
    xaxis=dict(title='Frequency  [Hz]', gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)'),
    yaxis=dict(title='|G(f)|', type='log', gridcolor='rgba(30,60,100,0.07)'),
)
fig.show()
```
